questions.prompt: Why does one full turn measure 2π radians?
questions.prompt_markup: Why does one full turn measure 2π radians?

choices.text: A full turn subtends the whole unit circle, whose circumference is 2π · 1 = 2π, and radian measure equals arc length on the unit circle.
Because π radians is a quarter turn of the unit circle, so a full turn of four quarters measures 2π radians.
Because the area of the unit circle is 2π · 1 = 2π, and radian measure equals the area swept out by the angle.
Because a full turn is 360°, and 360 = 2π when degrees are written as numbers of radians.

questions.correct_answer: A full turn subtends the whole unit circle, whose circumference is 2π · 1 = 2π, and radian measure equals arc length on the unit circle.
questions.grading_note: Radian measure is arc length on the unit circle. The others confuse degrees and radians, use the area (π), or misstate π as a quarter turn (it is a half turn).

questions.prompt: Why do cos θ and sin θ make sense for θ = 13π/6?
questions.prompt_markup: Why do cos θ and sin θ make sense for θ = 13π/6?

choices.text: 13π/6 ends at the same point as 13π/6 - π = 7π/6, so the values are those at 7π/6.
13π/6 = 2π + π/6 ends at the same point as π/6, so cos and sin take the values at that point.
13π/6 is greater than 2π, so cos and sin are both equal to 0 at that angle.
cos and sin are defined only for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, so 13π/6 is first divided by 13.

questions.correct_answer: 13π/6 = 2π + π/6 ends at the same point as π/6, so cos and sin take the values at that point.
questions.grading_note: Angles that differ by 2π end at the same point on the unit circle. The others subtract π (a half turn, the opposite point), claim both values are 0, or invent a rule that angles are divided down.
